title: Romeo Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Romeo wells have a 95 ft median depth; see local yields, water levels, drilling costs, permits and buyer risks.
h1: Wells and Water in Romeo, Colorado
intro_html:
For rural property around Romeo, the nearby well records point to generally moderate drilling depths and strong reported yields. The data covers permitted wells within five miles of Romeo in Conejos County, including older domestic wells and newer construction. It is useful for planning, but it does not guarantee what a new well will produce on one specific lot.

Most records are tied to an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer, with additional wells in the Confined San Luis Valley aquifer system. Check the nearest neighboring wells, the permit conditions, and the proposed septic and building layout before buying land or ordering a drill.

sections.heading: Romeo well depths vary, but most are not deep
sections.html:
The median recorded well depth near Romeo is 95 feet. The middle half runs from 50 to 120 feet, meaning many drilling bids should be based on a relatively shallow hole, while still allowing for local variation. About 52% of recorded wells are under 100 feet, and 38% fall from 100 to 300 feet.

Depths can change quickly across a valley or onto fractured ground. The deepest well in the records reaches 929 feet, and 8% are between 300 and 600 feet. A driller should price casing, grout, access, and the possibility of drilling beyond the local median rather than treating ninety-five feet as a guarantee.

sections.heading: Reported well yields around Romeo are generally solid
sections.html:
Among the wells that report a pump yield, the median is 15.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 12.0 and 15.0 gallons per minute. The reported mix is also favorable: 55% produce more than 15 gallons per minute, while 45% are in the 5 to 15 gallons per minute range.

No reported wells in this dataset fall under 1 gallon per minute or between 1 and 5 gallons per minute. That does not eliminate the risk of a weak new hole, because only 126 records report a pump yield. Ask for the well test, storage capacity, and permit use limits before relying on a yield number.

sections.heading: Romeo water levels and the recent measurement trend
sections.html:
Reported static water levels have a median depth of 25 feet below the surface. The middle half measures from 13 to 52 feet. A shallow static level can reduce pumping lift, but it is not the same as a guaranteed production rate. Water levels can differ with season, well location, pumping history, and the aquifer reached.

By measurement decade, the median depth to water changed from 20 feet in the 2010s to 30 feet in the 2020s. That suggests water was measured deeper in the more recent records, but it is not enough by itself to prove a regional decline. Only 79 wells report a static water level, so compare nearby wells and dates rather than relying on the median alone.

sections.heading: Permit history shows continuing drilling near Romeo
sections.html:
The records contain 1,007 permitted wells within five miles of Romeo. Of those, 779 are recorded as constructed and 784 report a total depth. Permits span from the 1950s through the newest permit year, 2025, so the area has a long local drilling history.

The busiest decades were the 1970s with 174 permits, the 2000s with 162, and the 2010s with 155. The most active names in these records are Heersink Drilling, Valley Pump Company, and Rocky Mountain Waterworks LLC. These records identify local activity, not an endorsement; confirm current licensing, insurance, scheduling, and references.

sections.heading: What a new Romeo well may cost to drill
sections.html:
For the mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground described in the local cost model, a typical drilling rate is $50 to $75 per foot. At the local median depth of 95 feet, the drilled hole works out to about $4,800 to $7,100. That figure is for drilling the hole, not the complete water system.

A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at about $10,800 to $19,100 at that median depth. The final bid can move with access, casing and grout requirements, formation changes, power distance, and treatment needs. Get the drilling rate and completion items in writing, including what happens if the hole must go deeper or does not produce enough water.

sections.heading: Risks to check before buying a Romeo lot
sections.html:
Low yield is not the main pattern in the reported data, but missing information matters: only 126 wells report a pump yield, and only 79 report a static water level. A dry hole or weak production remains possible on an untested parcel, particularly where the permit points to fractured bedrock. Confirm the nearest wells, their depths, their tests, and their current condition.

Water quality also deserves a test before closing. Mapped environmental data within about ten miles includes 1 PFAS sampling or contamination site and 1 EPA Superfund or cleanup site. There are 0 historic mine features mapped in that area. Keep the well, septic system, replacement area, driveway, and house site separated as required by the applicable county and state rules.

sections.heading: A practical plan for building near Romeo
sections.html:
Start with the Colorado Division of Water Resources permit search for the parcel and nearby wells. Review the permitted use carefully: the local use mix is 74% domestic or household, 35% stock, 11% irrigation, and 2% monitoring. A permit for household use is not automatically permission for every proposed use. Water rights, augmentation requirements, and basin rules can affect what you may legally do.

Before committing to land, have a driller review access from Romeo and nearby Manassa, Conejos, Antonito, La Jara, Sanford, or Capulin as relevant to the parcel. Price the well, pump, storage, power, trenching, and septic work together. For a new build, make the site plan around the well and septic setbacks first, then verify water quality and production after construction.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Romeo, Colorado?
faq.a: The median recorded well depth within five miles of Romeo is 95 feet. The middle half runs from 50 to 120 feet, and 52% are under 100 feet. Depth is not uniform: the deepest record is 929 feet, and 8% are between 300 and 600 feet. Nearby wells are the best guide for a specific parcel.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Romeo, Colorado?
faq.a: The local model uses $50 to $75 per foot for mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground. At Romeo’s 95-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $4,800 to $7,100. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $10,800 to $19,100. Access and deeper drilling can change the bid.

faq.q: Do Romeo wells produce enough water?
faq.a: Among the 126 wells reporting a pump yield, the median is 15.0 gallons per minute and the middle half is 12.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. Reported yields show 55% above 15 gallons per minute and 45% from 5 to 15. Because many permits do not report a yield, test the individual well before relying on it.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Romeo?
faq.a: The permit records do not establish that every Romeo well is safe to drink. Test a private well for common bacteria, minerals, and any concerns identified by the site history. Mapped environmental data within about ten miles includes one PFAS sampling or contamination site and one EPA Superfund or cleanup site, so a property-specific water test is important before closing.

faq.q: Are water levels dropping near Romeo, Colorado?
faq.a: Reported median static water level was 20 feet below the surface in the 2010s and 30 feet in the 2020s. That points to deeper recent measurements, but it does not prove a regional decline because only 79 wells report static water levels and conditions vary by location and season. Compare measurements from nearby wells with similar construction and dates.
